cli-skill.description: Every CLI command has an agent skill that names its invocation (D94), so a coding agent finds the command when it needs it.
cli-skill.rationale: Help text is loaded only once an agent already knows the command, while a skill is loaded when the task matches its description, so a command with no skill is invisible to an agent that has not heard of it. One level is enough: maintainer-skill scores the skill file itself.

has-skill.fix: Add plugins/toolbox-operator/skills/<slug>/SKILL.md that includes the invocation toolbox <command>, with the flags and the exit codes.
has-skill.rationale: An agent that cannot find a command will not run it. The skill routes a coding agent to the invocation when its task calls for it; matching the leaf name keeps nested commands from hiding behind their parent.

cli-skill.title: Every CLI command has a skill

maintainer-action-deps.description: Each third-party action across every workflow that uses it: pinned to a commit SHA everywhere (D70, docs/design/github-actions-standards.md).
maintainer-action-deps.rationale: A compromised action reaches every workflow that runs it, so in an incident the question is which workflows use it and at which refs. Scoring per action answers that and shows any use still unpinned; bronze is the only level because an action is either pinned everywhere or not.

pinned-everywhere.fix: Pin this action to a full commit SHA in every workflow that uses it. Resolve the tag with `git ls-remote https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> refs/tags/<tag>` and peel an annotated tag (`^{}`) so the SHA is the commit.
pinned-everywhere.rationale: One unpinned use is enough for a moved tag to run new code with that workflow's token, so an action counts as pinned only when every workflow pins it.

maintainer-action-deps.title: Third-party actions pinned

maintainer-agent-doc.description: Each agent instruction file: one canonical AGENTS.md with aliases pointing at it, links and commands that work in CI, and no hidden text or credentials (D75, D82, D83).

links.title: Decision: agent instruction files are scored

maintainer-agent-doc.rationale: Agents load these files as standing instructions for every change to the repository, and a second, divergent copy is followed by one harness and ignored by another. Bronze is one source whose links work, plus the two safety items; silver says how to test and fits in context; gold points at the decision log and names only checks CI runs.

checks-run-in-ci.fix: Run each command in the evidence from a GitHub Actions workflow, or remove it from the check procedure. Commands that appear only in a markdown table are the track index and are not required.

links.title: Decision: named commands run in CI

checks-run-in-ci.rationale: A check that agents are told to run but CI never runs can break without anyone noticing, and passing it locally then proves nothing CI agrees with.

has-commands.fix: Name the build or test command in AGENTS.md (cargo, npm, pnpm, yarn, pytest, or toolbox). An alias inherits the canonical file's commands.
has-commands.rationale: An agent that is not told how to build and test guesses, and either skips verification or runs the wrong check.

links-resolve.fix: Fix or remove the relative links in the evidence. An agent follows them.
links-resolve.rationale: Instruction files push detail into linked documents; a broken link leaves the agent without the rule it was sent to read.

names-the-decision-log.fix: Link the canonical AGENTS.md at the decision log, so an agent edits the log instead of treating this file as the only source of truth.
names-the-decision-log.rationale: AGENTS.md summarises; the decision log is the source of truth. An agent that never learns of the log acts on a summary that may be stale and records new decisions in the wrong place.

no-hardcoded-secrets.fix: Remove the credential in the evidence. An instruction file is loaded into the agent's prompt.
no-hardcoded-secrets.rationale: The file is committed to the repository and loaded into every agent's prompt, so a credential in it is exposed to every reader and every transcript. It sits at bronze so such a file cannot pass the ratchet.

no-hidden-instructions.fix: Remove zero-width and other default-ignorable characters, bidi controls and variation selectors outside emoji from the file. They are invisible to a reviewer and visible to a model.
no-hidden-instructions.rationale: Hidden characters let text reach the model that a reviewer never sees, a way to slip instructions past review into every session. It sits at bronze so such a file cannot pass the ratchet.

single-source.fix: Keep instructions in AGENTS.md. An alias such as CLAUDE.md should link to it, not restate a second set of rules.
single-source.rationale: Harnesses read different filenames; when an alias restates the rules instead of pointing at AGENTS.md, the copies drift and agents in different harnesses follow different rules.

within-budget.fix: Keep the file under 500 lines. Move detail into a linked document. The agents.md v1.1 proposal uses 500 lines as the point where a file should be split.
within-budget.rationale: The file is loaded into every session's context, so its length is paid on every task and crowds out the work. 500 lines is a proposal's guideline, not a ratified limit.

maintainer-agent-doc.title: Agent instruction files

maintainer-benchmark.description: Each DX Benchmark: declared, pre-registered against a rival on pinned open-source repositories, and run with results and the fixes it produced (D01M82X2K0DYWTCA23MQJ4CKR0Z).
maintainer-benchmark.rationale: A claim that Toolbox makes a lifecycle easier for agents is only as good as the benchmark behind it, and two benchmarks without repeated runs or an independent adjudicator reached wrong results. The levels follow a benchmark's life: declared, then registered so the result can't be explained away, then run, published and turned into fixes.

closes-the-loop.fix: List what the benchmark changed in Toolbox: the friction fixes and the decisions it produced (dx-benchmarks.md §4, step 10).
closes-the-loop.rationale: Measured friction is a benchmark's most useful output; a run that changed nothing in Toolbox paid its token cost without making Toolbox better.

declared.fix: Give the entry a one-sentence question, the SDLC layers it measures (maintainer, package-author, operator, user) and a status (designed, blocked, complete, archived).
declared.rationale: Without a question and the layers it measures, a benchmark can't be tied to a decision or to the SDLC stages it is meant to prove; a benchmark with no decision behind it is a demo.

has-a-rival.fix: Name the arm without Toolbox: an agent from scratch, a checklist, hand-written glue, an existing standard or another platform (dx-benchmarks.md §4, step 3).
has-a-rival.rationale: Beating a straw man proves nothing; a win counts only against the alternative a capable team would really use, which our record shows is often an agent with a checklist.

method-registered.fix: Before it runs, register it under protocol 2: set protocol 2, commit the prompts, plan at least three runs per arm, name the measure a dry run showed the runtime reports, and name a designer and a different adjudicator (dx-benchmarks.md §4.1).
method-registered.rationale: connector-ab's win came from tuning only Toolbox's arm, and deploy-ab's defeat from probes that treated the arms unequally, both judged by their designers. Registering the method before the run closes those routes.

open-source-pinned.fix: Run on open-source repositories we didn't write and list each as owner/name@commit, so the run can be reproduced.
open-source-pinned.rationale: Repositories we wrote can be tuned to Toolbox, and an unpinned one changes under the run; forks of others' code at a pinned commit keep the work real and the result reproducible.

paths-exist.fix: Point readme at the benchmark's pre-registration and results at its published results, as paths that exist in the repository.
paths-exist.rationale: The catalog entry is the index to the pre-registered bar and the published result; a dead path means neither can be read or checked against the other.

pre-registered.fix: Name the hypotheses the benchmark tests, each with a bar written in its README before it ran (dx-benchmarks.md §4, step 5).
pre-registered.rationale: A bar set after the run bends to fit the result; without one, both of the standards A/B's losses could have been explained away as learning cost.

results-recorded.fix: Run it, then record the outcome against the bar as written and the path of the published results (dx-benchmarks.md §4, step 9).
results-recorded.rationale: A loss we hide is a loss we repeat; until the outcome is published against the bar as written, the benchmark is evidence of nothing.

says-why.fix: Say why an archived benchmark has served its value (servedValue), or what a blocked one waits on (blockedOn).
says-why.rationale: An archived benchmark without its reason looks abandoned, and a blocked one without its prerequisite can't be unblocked; the reason is what the next maintainer acts on.

sound-method.fix: Rerun it under protocol 2 and record the frozen commit, the spread across at least three runs per arm, and the independent adjudicator's fit audit (dx-benchmarks.md §4.1). A protocol-1 result stays on the record as one sample.
sound-method.rationale: One run is one sample: an unchanged rival's calls moved by 21 across connector-ab's rounds. A result supports a claim only with a frozen commit, the spread of repeated runs and an audit of what changed between rounds.

maintainer-benchmark.title: DX Benchmarks

maintainer-ci-reliability.description: Whether green CI means good on the default branch: failures visible and counted, including those a re-run hid, every job bounded by a timeout, and a branch that rarely fails (D70; docs/design/thresholds.md for the tiers). Speed is maintainer-ci-speed.
maintainer-ci-reliability.rationale: CI is only worth running if red means something broke and green means nothing did; flaky, hidden or hung jobs teach people to ignore it. Bronze makes failures visible and bounded and keeps the branch out of long red streaks; silver and gold each halve the share of first-try failures a reader must check, over enough runs to tell the tiers apart.

every-job-has-timeout.fix: Set `timeout-minutes` on every job; the default is 360 minutes of a hung runner.
every-job-has-timeout.rationale: Without `timeout-minutes` a hung job holds a runner for GitHub's default of 360 minutes before it fails, spending runner time and delaying the signal everyone is waiting for.

fail-rate-under-10.fix: Open the failed runs in the evidence and classify each cause: a flaky test (fix or quarantine it in its test file), infrastructure (pin or retry the step in the workflow file), or real breakage merged to the branch (add the missing check to the pull request workflow).
fail-rate-under-10.rationale: At silver, failures are rare enough that each can be classified as a flake, infrastructure or a break a pull request check missed. It needs a minimum number of runs, because with few runs one failure moves the rate across tiers.

fail-rate-under-20.fix: Open the failed runs in the evidence, find the failing jobs, and fix their causes in the code or the workflow file. The rate is over the last runs on the branch, so it falls as passing runs replace failed ones. Re-running a failure doesn't help: a run that passed on a later attempt counts as failed, continue-on-error, `|| true` and skips on the default branch are caught by failures-visible, and cancelled runs are shown here.
fail-rate-under-20.rationale: Every red run costs someone a look, and a re-run that turns it green hides a flaky test or step; counting first-try failures stops re-runs from lowering the rate. Bronze is the first step for a branch that fails often.

fail-rate-under-5.fix: Open each failed run in the evidence and fix its cause where it lives (the test, the workflow file, or the check the pull request lacked), so that every failure on the branch is rare enough to be looked at.
fail-rate-under-5.rationale: At gold, a red run on the default branch is rare enough that every one is looked at and fixed at its cause, so red keeps its meaning.

failures-visible.fix: For each listed job or step in the workflow file: remove `continue-on-error`, `|| true` (or `set +e`), or the `if:` that skips it on the default branch. If a step is expected to fail, give it an `id:` and check `steps.<id>.outcome` in a later step, so the failure is still asserted.
failures-visible.rationale: `continue-on-error`, `|| true`, `set +e` and a skip on the default branch each turn a failure into a pass, so the fail-rate rules would count it green. It is their prerequisite, so it sits at bronze.

main-not-stuck-red.fix: Fix the default branch before anything else: open the failed runs in the evidence, find the failing job, and fix its cause in the code or in the workflow file under .github/workflows/.
main-not-stuck-red.rationale: A default branch that keeps failing breaks everyone who branches from it, and each new failure hides behind the last. Three in a row means the break is not being fixed.

still-running.fix: Re-enable the workflow (`gh workflow enable <file>`, or the Actions tab), or delete its file from .github/workflows/ if it is retired.
still-running.rationale: A disabled workflow's old run history still reads green, so it would pass every run-history rule while checking nothing. GitHub disables scheduled workflows in a public repository after 60 days without activity, and anyone can disable one by hand. A workflow whose triggers simply stop matching stays active and is not caught here.

maintainer-ci-reliability.title: CI reliability

maintainer-ci-security.description: What an attacker could do through a workflow: pinned actions, least- privilege tokens, no risky triggers with write access, and zizmor and actionlint clean (D70, docs/design/github-actions-standards.md).
maintainer-ci-security.rationale: A workflow runs with the repository's token and secrets, so a hijacked action, an injected expression or an over-broad token is a route to pushing code or stealing credentials. Bronze closes the direct routes, silver removes write access where untrusted events arrive, and gold leaves nothing zizmor flags unexplained.

actionlint-clean.fix: Fix what actionlint reports (`actionlint` in the repository root).
actionlint-clean.rationale: A syntax error, a mistyped expression or a wrong action input only shows up when the workflow runs, and actionlint also finds script injection; catching these in the file is cheaper than a broken run.

least-privilege-token.fix: Declare `permissions:` at the top of the workflow (read-only, e.g. `contents: read`) and grant writes per job.
least-privilege-token.rationale: A job without `permissions:` gets the token's default scopes, which can include write access, so any compromised step can push code or change releases. Read-only by default limits what one bad step can do.

no-high-findings.fix: Fix zizmor's high-severity findings (`zizmor --offline .github/workflows actions`); see https://docs.zizmor.sh/audits/.
no-high-findings.rationale: zizmor's high-severity audits, such as template injection and dangerous triggers, find ways for untrusted input to run code with the workflow's token. One is enough for an attacker, so they belong in the floor.

no-medium-findings.fix: Fix zizmor's medium findings (e.g. `artipacked`: set `persist-credentials: false` on checkout).
no-medium-findings.rationale: Medium findings widen what one compromised step can reach: a checkout token left in `.git/config`, for example, is readable by every later step and by any artifact that uploads the directory.

no-write-tokens-on-risky-triggers.fix: Don't combine pull_request_target/workflow_run/issue_comment with write permissions; split privileged steps into a separate workflow.
no-write-tokens-on-risky-triggers.rationale: These triggers run in the base repository's context on events outsiders can cause, such as a fork's pull request or a comment, so a write token there puts a privileged credential within reach of untrusted input.

pinned-to-sha.fix: Pin every third-party `uses:` to a full commit SHA. Resolve the tag with `git ls-remote https://github.com/<owner>/<repo> refs/tags/<tag>` and peel an annotated tag (`^{}`) so the SHA is the commit, then put the tag in a comment. Let Dependabot update them.
pinned-to-sha.rationale: A tag or branch can be moved to new code after review, and that code runs with the workflow's token and secrets; only a commit SHA fixes what runs.

zizmor-clean.fix: Resolve or explicitly ignore (with a reason) zizmor's low and informational findings.
zizmor-clean.rationale: Low and informational findings are weak signals one by one, but each fixed or ignored with a written reason lets a reviewer tell a known trade-off from an oversight. That is polish beyond the direct risks, so it is gold.

maintainer-ci-security.title: CI security

maintainer-ci-speed.description: Whether CI answers quickly and spends no runner time on superseded commits: a cost and feedback-time concern, separate from whether CI can be trusted (maintainer-ci-reliability; docs/design/thresholds.md).
maintainer-ci-speed.rationale: Slow runs and runs for superseded commits cost runner minutes and queue time, and make people wait or switch task for feedback. Speed is not a correctness or security property, so it has its own card rather than holding a reliable workflow back.

cancels-superseded-runs.fix:
Add, at the top of the workflow file:
  concurrency:
    group: "${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}"
    cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
A new push to a pull request then cancels its old run, while every
run on main still finishes.
cancels-superseded-runs.rationale: Without a concurrency group per ref, each push to a pull request starts a new run while the old one, whose result no longer matters, keeps a runner busy.

fast-feedback.fix: Keep the p90 run under 15 minutes: split slow jobs, cache builds, move long suites off the PR path.
fast-feedback.rationale: Past the bound, developers switch to other work while they wait and come back late to a failure. The bound is a chosen point, not a measured one.

maintainer-ci-speed.title: CI speed

maintainer-connector.description: Each first-party connector: configurable, speaking the protocol the conformance kit checks, and free of credentials in shipped code (D73, docs/design/connector-standards.md).
maintainer-connector.rationale: Connectors hold credentials to upstream systems and feed every entity a portal derives, so one that is undocumented, off-protocol or carrying a secret harms every portal that runs it. Bronze is a connector an operator can configure, silver has the message shapes the conformance kit checks plus a test, and gold runs in CI with no credential in the tree. Lag and error rate need a live portal and are not gated.

closes-snapshots.fix: End every resync kind with a `snapshot_complete` message. A push-only connector is exempt: it has no resync.
closes-snapshots.rationale: A resync is the only command that can remove records by omission, and only once the snapshot is closed; without `snapshot_complete`, records deleted upstream stay in the catalog.

config-documented.fix: Document the configuration in the crate doc: TOOLBOX_CONNECTOR_CONFIG for an in-image connector, or the --toolbox and --listen flags for a remote one.
config-documented.rationale: A connector reads its settings from TOOLBOX_CONNECTOR_CONFIG or its flags; when they are undocumented an operator has to read the source to wire it into a manifest.

described.fix: Add a Cargo.toml description and a //! crate doc that says what the connector emits.
described.rationale: An operator choosing a connector reads its package description and crate docs, not its source; without them they cannot tell what it emits.

exercised-in-ci.fix: Run toolbox connector test on this binary from CI. A push-only connector has no resync for that kit; an acceptance script must start it instead.
exercised-in-ci.rationale: The conformance kit is the run that proves the protocol shapes the static rules infer; a connector CI never starts can drift from the protocol unnoticed.

has-tests.fix: Add a unit test that does not need the upstream API: a parser, a record shape, or a capabilities case.
has-tests.rationale: A unit test that needs no upstream API runs on every build without credentials, so a parser or record-shape regression fails CI instead of a portal's next sync.

names-its-kinds.fix: Name each record kind in the connector's source (in a `record` or `snapshot_complete` message) or, for a generic runner, say in its `//!` crate doc that kinds come from the job config.
names-its-kinds.rationale: An operator must declare a connector's kinds in the manifest, and the conformance kit rejects capabilities that name undeclared ones; unnamed kinds leave both to guesswork.

no-hardcoded-secrets.fix: Remove the hardcoded credentials in the evidence. Read tokens from the environment or from TOOLBOX_CONNECTOR_CONFIG.

links.title: Thresholds: why credentials sit at bronze

no-hardcoded-secrets.rationale: Connectors are open source and carry tokens for systems such as GitHub, so a credential in the tree is published with it. It sits at bronze so such a connector cannot pass the ratchet.

reports-missing-ids.fix: Send `not_found` when a refresh names an unknown external id. A push-only connector is exempt: the provider sends deletes.
reports-missing-ids.rationale: A refresh never deletes by omission, so without `not_found` an entity deleted upstream stays in the catalog and the requester sees it as unresolved.

speaks-the-protocol.fix: Serve commands with run_stdio (in-image) or run_remote (long-poll). A connector that does neither is not on the control channel.
speaks-the-protocol.rationale: Toolbox asks connectors for data only over the control channel; a connector that serves neither stdio nor long-poll can never be told to refresh or resync.

maintainer-connector.title: First-party connectors

maintainer-crate.description: Each Rust crate: documented, tested with assertions and enough tests for its size, passing, clippy-clean, and kept small and simple (D65, docs/design/toolbox-for-toolbox.md).
maintainer-crate.rationale: Crates are the code Toolbox ships, and a person or an agent can only change one safely if it says what it is, has tests that can fail, passes them, and is made of functions small enough to read. Bronze is what makes a change checkable at all; silver and gold tighten documentation, size and complexity in steps, with the numbers in the manifest so raising them is a reviewed change.

bounded-complexity.fix: Simplify the functions in the evidence (extract match arms, early returns).
bounded-complexity.rationale: Cyclomatic complexity counts the independent paths through a function, and each needs a test of its own; past the bound a function has more paths than its tests are likely to cover.

clippy-clean.fix: Fix the clippy warnings in the evidence (`cargo clippy -p <crate> --all-targets`).
clippy-clean.rationale: Clippy's lints catch common bugs and unidiomatic code before review, and CI runs it with `-D warnings`, so a warning here would fail the build anyway.

crate-docs.fix: Start the crate's `src/lib.rs` or `src/main.rs` with `//!` docs: what it is and which spec section it implements.
crate-docs.rationale: The crate doc is what a reader or an agent sees first when deciding whether to touch a crate; without it, the crate's purpose and the spec section it implements have to be worked out from the code.

few-unwraps.fix: At most one unwrap/expect per 100 lines outside tests: return errors or document the invariant.

links.title: The Rust Book: to panic! or not to panic!

few-unwraps.rationale: Each unwrap or expect outside tests panics if its assumption fails, crashing the process instead of returning an error the caller can handle; keeping them rare makes each one a deliberate invariant.

fully-documented.fix: Document every item in the evidence.
fully-documented.rationale: At gold no public item has to be read in source to be used, so an agent can work with the crate through its API without loading its internals.

has-tests.fix: Add a #[test] for the crate's main behaviour (or an integration test in tests/), and give each listed test an assert: a test that checks nothing passes whatever the code does.
has-tests.rationale: A crate without tests can change behaviour with nothing failing, and a test that asserts nothing gives the same false confidence while looking like coverage.

no-huge-functions.fix: Split the functions in the evidence into named steps.
no-huge-functions.rationale: A very long function is hard to review and can't be tested in parts, so a change inside it risks effects far from the edit. Silver catches the outliers; gold's short-functions tightens the limit.

public-api-documented.fix: Add /// docs to the public items in the evidence.
public-api-documented.rationale: Other crates and agents use a crate through its public items; an undocumented one makes them read the implementation, which a public API is meant to spare them.

short-functions.fix: Keep functions at 80 lines or fewer; split those in the evidence.
short-functions.rationale: A function short enough to read in one sitting can be reviewed, tested and replaced as a unit; longer ones usually mix several steps that deserve names of their own.

simple-functions.fix: Keep cyclomatic complexity at 15 or lower; simplify those in the evidence.
simple-functions.rationale: At the gold bound a function has few enough paths that each can be tested and reasoned about; more branching than that is usually clearer as named helpers.

tests-pass.fix: Run `cargo test -p <crate>` and fix the failures in the evidence. Remove `#[ignore]` from ignored tests, and the always-false `#[cfg(...)]` from listed tests, and make them pass: a test that doesn't run checks nothing. Tests that need OpenFGA run with TOOLBOX_REQUIRE_OPENFGA set, so install it (TOOLBOX_OPENFGA_BIN) rather than letting them skip.
tests-pass.rationale: A failing, ignored or compiled-out test checks nothing, and an ignored one hides its failure from everyone; an authorization test that quietly skips without OpenFGA would let authorization changes through untested.

tests-scale-with-code.fix: Add tests for the crate's untested behaviour until it has at least 2 per 1,000 code lines (docs/design/thresholds.md says why 2).
tests-scale-with-code.rationale: One test meets bronze however large a crate grows; a floor per thousand lines, set from the spread across this workspace, flags crates that are untested or nearly so. It is a floor, not a coverage target.

maintainer-crate.title: Rust crates

maintainer-dependency.description: Each direct Cargo dependency: a bounded requirement from a registry, locked to one version across the workspace, and shared ones inherited from the workspace (D74).
maintainer-dependency.rationale: Every direct dependency is code the binary runs, so it should come from a known source and resolve the same way on every build. Bronze bounds the requirement and the source, silver locks one version, and gold declares a shared dependency once so its users can't drift; advisories and licences need a database and a policy, so they don't gate.

from-a-registry.fix: Depend on a crates.io release. A git dependency is not reproducible from the registry and is not reviewed here.
from-a-registry.rationale: A git source is code from a repository rather than a published release, so the build can't be reproduced from the registry alone; cargo-deny's `[sources]` check flags it for the same reason.

locked.fix: Run `cargo generate-lockfile` so `Cargo.lock` records this dependency. The lockfile is what makes the build reproducible.
locked.rationale: `Cargo.lock` is Rust's pin: without it every build resolves versions afresh, and two builds of one commit can differ. OpenSSF Scorecard accepts the lockfile as the pin for Rust.

one-version.fix: The lockfile resolves this crate to more than one version. Move the direct requirement onto the newer release, or drop the dependency that pulls the other one in.
one-version.rationale: Two versions of one crate are both compiled into the binary, which lengthens the build, and their types don't match across the copies; cargo-deny bans duplicate versions for the same reason.

shared-is-inherited.fix: Declare this dependency once in [workspace.dependencies] and inherit it. It is used by more than one crate, so two requirements can drift.
shared-is-inherited.rationale: When each crate writes its own requirement for a shared dependency, the requirements drift apart and the lockfile can end up with two versions; one entry in `[workspace.dependencies]` keeps them together.

version-bounded.fix: Replace the requirement in the evidence with a caret, tilde or exact version. An empty requirement, *, or a bare >= has no ceiling.
version-bounded.rationale: A requirement without a ceiling accepts any future major release, so a `cargo update` or a fresh resolve can pull in breaking changes nobody chose.

maintainer-dependency.title: Cargo dependencies

maintainer-docs.description: Each design and reference doc: links that resolve, its SDLC layer named, cited decisions that exist, a status banner and its sources (D84).
maintainer-docs.rationale: Agents read these docs as the source of intent, so a dead link, an unnamed SDLC layer or a decision id that names no file sends them to the wrong place or nowhere. Bronze is the pointers; silver is what lets a reader trust a design doc: what is decided and built, and where its claims come from.

cited-decisions-exist.fix: The decision ids in the evidence are not files in docs/decisions/. Cite one that exists, or add the file. Mint the id with python3 scripts/decision-id.py.
cited-decisions-exist.rationale: Decision files are the source of truth for what is decided. A cited id with no file makes a claim look settled when a reader cannot check what, if anything, was decided.

cites-sources.fix: End the design doc with a `## Sources` section (AGENTS.md working rules).
cites-sources.rationale: Design docs make claims about other tools, standards and vendors. A Sources section lets a reader check them against primary sources instead of taking them on trust.

links-resolve.fix: Fix or remove the relative links in the evidence.
links-resolve.rationale: A file move or rename breaks the links to it without failing any build, and the reader who follows one loses the context the doc relies on.

names-sdlc-layer.fix: Say which SDLC you mean: maintainer, operator or user (docs/sdlc.md, D63).
names-sdlc-layer.rationale: Toolbox has four SDLC layers with different builders and checks, so a bare "SDLC" leaves the reader to guess whose loop the doc is about.

status-banner.fix: Start the design doc under `docs/design/` with a `*Status:*` line saying what is decided and what is built.
status-banner.rationale: A design doc mixes decided, built and deferred material. Without the banner a reader or agent can implement something that was deferred, and where the banner and the body disagree the banner wins.

maintainer-docs.title: Design and reference docs

maintainer-example.description: Each example and experiment write-up agents copy: links that resolve, the check it names, and no credentials (D78, docs/design/example-standards.md).
maintainer-example.rationale: Agents copy examples as working patterns, so a write-up that cannot be followed or checked spreads its mistakes into every copy. Bronze is a write-up a reader can follow; silver names the command that proves it still works; gold ties it to the design so it does not become a second source of truth.

cites-the-design.fix: Link the write-up at the design doc (`docs/design/<topic>.md`) or the decision (`docs/decisions/<id>.md`) it demonstrates, so the example is not a second source of truth.
cites-the-design.rationale: An example that does not point at its design drifts from it unnoticed, and a reader cannot tell which of the two to believe.

has-a-heading.fix: Start the write-up with a level-1 heading (`# Name`) that names the example.
has-a-heading.rationale: The heading is the example's name. Without one, a reader scanning the examples, or an agent choosing one to copy, cannot tell what it demonstrates.

links-resolve.fix: Fix or remove the relative links in the evidence. An agent follows them to the files the example depends on.
links-resolve.rationale: A missing target means the write-up has drifted from the files it describes, so a copy made from it is incomplete or wrong.

no-hardcoded-secrets.fix: Remove the credential in the evidence. An example is copied and read by agents.
no-hardcoded-secrets.rationale: Examples are published with the repository and copied verbatim, so a credential in one is exposed to every reader and can end up reused in their own setup.

says-how-to-check.fix: Name the command that checks this example (toolbox, cargo, npm, python, fga, or a ./run script). A reader should be able to reproduce it.
says-how-to-check.rationale: An example nobody can run is a claim, not a procedure. Naming the check lets a reader confirm it still works before copying it, as the reference portal's checks do for v1.

maintainer-example.title: Examples and experiments

maintainer-observability.description: Toolbox's runtime telemetry checklist: the OTel crate, metric catalog, structured logs, alert stubs and an exported trace, each a file that exists (docs/design/observability.md).
maintainer-observability.rationale: Operators can't run a portal they can't see: without traces, metrics and logs under a stable contract, connector lag or a stuck snapshot goes unnoticed. Bronze is the crate and catalog that keep Prometheus and OTLP names from drifting, silver adds logs, alerts and a reviewed monitor stage, and gold a trace exported to a real collector.

assessed-monitor.rationale: Every file can exist while the operator's monitor stage still can't be carried out by an agent; only a review against sdlc-stage-quality judges that.

metric-catalog-complete.fix: Add METRIC_CATALOG.md listing the v1 required metric names (v1-spec §10.5).
metric-catalog-complete.rationale: Metric names, units and labels are part of Toolbox's SemVer surface, and operators' dashboards and alerts depend on them; without a written catalog a rename breaks them silently.

operator-monitor-alerts.fix: Add alert rule stubs under ops/alerts/ for snapshot lag and index freshness (Grafana pack may come later).
operator-monitor-alerts.rationale: Metrics nobody alerts on are noticed only after users notice; snapshot lag and index freshness are the signals that a portal is serving stale data.

otel-crate-present.fix: Add crates/toolbox-telemetry to the workspace with opentelemetry dependencies (plan §4, D6).
otel-crate-present.rationale: Without one crate that owns the bootstrap, each crate sets up its own exporters and metric names drift between Prometheus and OTLP.

otlp-export-tested.fix: Add experiments/otel-testbed with otelcol-contrib and a scoring script (implementation step 5).
otlp-export-tested.rationale: Unit tests can pass while nothing reaches a collector; exporting to a pinned otelcol-contrib is what proves the OTLP contract that operators' backends depend on.

prom-endpoint.fix: Add a unit/integration test that asserts metrics_text() contains the catalog names (including toolbox_snapshot_lag_seconds).
prom-endpoint.rationale: A catalog protects operators only if `/metrics` really serves it; a test pinning the names catches a dropped or renamed metric before it ships.

service-name-documented.fix: Document OTEL_SERVICE_NAME / service.name in the telemetry crate README.
service-name-documented.rationale: Backends group every signal by `service.name`; an operator who doesn't know to set it sees Toolbox's telemetry under a generic default, mixed with other services.

structured-logs.fix: Add a test that init with JSON log format succeeds, and route connector/snapshot failures through tracing instead of eprintln.
structured-logs.rationale: Plain stderr lines can't be queried or joined to a trace; JSON logs carrying the trace id let an operator follow a failure from its log line to the request that caused it.

maintainer-observability.title: Runtime observability

maintainer-openssf.description: OpenSSF Scorecard's checks, as Scorecard scores them. Its one level, ten, means a check scores 10 out of 10. The box adds only the ratchet: a check's gap to 10 is the measure, so a score that drops fails a pull request and one that rises is an improvement. A check Scorecard adds in a new release doesn't fail the gate.
maintainer-openssf.rationale: OpenSSF Scorecard is an established, openly governed standard for supply-chain security, so the portal carries its checks as OpenSSF defines them rather than writing weaker copies that would compete with it. Its one level is Scorecard's own maximum, and the ratchet stops any check from falling while the gap is paid down.

ten.fix: Follow the check's documentation (in the evidence). The check, its scoring and its remediation are OpenSSF's.
ten.rationale: Each point below 10 is a supply-chain weakness OpenSSF documents with its risk and remediation; holding every check at its current score keeps a regression from slipping in unnoticed.

maintainer-openssf.title: OpenSSF Scorecard

maintainer-package.description: Each npm manifest we keep: private when it is an application, locked, and free of credentials, so installs are reproducible (docs/design/package-standards.md).
maintainer-package.rationale: These manifests decide what code npm installs into the builds this repository runs, so an unbounded range, a git dependency or a missing lockfile lets that code change without a review. Bronze bounds what can be installed; silver pins it and gives CI something to run; gold makes the package self-describing and has CI install exactly the lockfile.

ci-installs-from-the-lockfile.fix: Change this package's CI install in `.github/workflows/` to `npm ci`, or to `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`. Those commands install the lockfile as written and do not rewrite it.
ci-installs-from-the-lockfile.rationale: An unlocked install can update the lockfile during the job, so CI tests a dependency set that no commit records, and the lockfile's pins protect nothing.

described.fix: Add a description. npm's package.json document says to put a description in it, so a reader can tell packages apart.
described.rationale: Without a description a reader has to open the code to learn what a package is for, which matters most in a repository with several.

engines-declared.fix: Set engines.node to the Node version this package is developed with. That is the field npm documents for the runtime.
engines-declared.rationale: Without engines.node the supported runtime is unwritten, so a contributor or a CI image on another Node version hits failures that look like bugs in the code.

from-a-registry.fix: Depend on a registry version. The evidence names a git URL or a tarball URL instead of a version the registry serves.
from-a-registry.rationale: A git or tarball URL skips the registry: no version range bounds it, and whoever controls that host or branch decides what gets installed.

has-a-check.fix: Add a test, build, check or typecheck script. npm's guidance is to keep a smoke test, and this repository runs build and check in CI.
has-a-check.rationale: A package with no test, build or check script gives CI nothing to run, so a change that breaks it can merge unnoticed.

locked.fix: Commit a lockfile beside package.json, or a workspace-root pnpm-lock.yaml / yarn.lock that covers this package. package-lock.json records an integrity hash for every installed package.
locked.rationale: Without a lockfile every install resolves the ranges again, so two builds of the same commit can get different code, including transitive dependencies nobody chose.

named.fix: Set name in package.json. npm uses it as the package identity, including when the package is private.
named.rationale: Lockfiles, workspaces and every report refer to a package by its name; an unnamed manifest cannot be depended on or told apart.

no-hardcoded-secrets.fix: Remove the credential in the evidence. The manifest is committed and read by the installer.
no-hardcoded-secrets.rationale: A credential in a committed manifest is readable by everyone with access to the repository and stays in its history after it is removed, so it has to be revoked.

publish-intent.fix: Set private to true for a package this repository does not publish, or set version before publishing. npm refuses to publish a private package.
publish-intent.rationale: A public package with no version is neither protected from an accidental npm publish nor ready for a deliberate one. Marking an application private states that it is not meant for the registry.

version-bounded.fix: Replace the ranges in the evidence. A star, x, latest or unbounded minimum can move without a review. Caret and tilde ranges stay bounded.
version-bounded.rationale: An unbounded range resolves to whatever the registry serves at install time, so a breaking major version or a compromised release can enter the build with no change to review.

maintainer-package.title: npm manifests

maintainer-plugin.description: Each agent plugin package we ship: a valid Agent Plugins 1.0.0 manifest an agent harness can install, with its skills scored by maintainer-skill (docs/design/plugin-standards.md).
maintainer-plugin.rationale: The package is what a plugin manager installs into an agent harness: a manifest that breaks Agent Plugins 1.0.0 is not installed at all, and a credential pasted into it ships to every machine that installs it. Bronze is installable, silver declares the MCP server portably, and gold keeps credentials and paths inside the package. Loading it in each harness is not gated.

manifest-valid.fix: Point $schema at the 1.0.0 plugin schema, use a name of 1–64 lowercase letters, digits, dots and hyphens, and write a description.
manifest-valid.rationale: The 1.0.0 manifest schema is closed and the name has a fixed grammar, so a plugin manager that validates the manifest rejects the whole package, skills included, when either is off.

mcp-declared.fix: Add mcp.json next to plugin.json with the 1.0.0 mcp schema. A tool that exists only in a vendor config is a harness lock-in.
mcp-declared.rationale: An MCP server declared only in one vendor's config works in that harness alone; mcp.json is the place every compliant harness reads.

no-hardcoded-secrets.fix: Remove the credential in the evidence from plugin.json or mcp.json.
no-hardcoded-secrets.rationale: plugin.json and mcp.json are published with the package, so a credential in either reaches every install. It sits at bronze so such a package cannot pass the ratchet.

no-secret-headers.fix: Remove the secret in the evidence. MCP authorization is client-managed. Headers must not carry credentials.
no-secret-headers.rationale: The spec forbids credentials in headers because MCP authorization is client-managed; a token there ships to everyone who installs the package.

paths-stay-inside.fix: Drop the .. segments in the evidence. Plugin paths stay inside the plugin root.
paths-stay-inside.rationale: A `..` path reaches files the package does not contain, so it breaks once installed elsewhere and can run or read whatever sits beside the install.

portable-components.fix: Move each skill to skills/<name>/SKILL.md. Client-specific files go under a reverse-domain directory, not beside the manifest.
portable-components.rationale: Agent Plugins 1.0.0 has exactly two portable component types at fixed locations; a skill anywhere else is not part of the package for a compliant harness.

stdio-command.fix: Set command to one token (./bin/toolbox-mcp or ${PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/tool). Do not use a shell string.
stdio-command.rationale: The spec requires one token so the harness can start the server without a shell; a shell string depends on which shell runs it and lets one field chain extra commands.

maintainer-plugin.title: Agent plugin packages

maintainer-python.description: Every file ruff checks is clean. The measure is its findings, so a new finding is a regression and a fixed one an improvement; a new file must arrive clean.
maintainer-python.rationale: A tool's findings help only if new ones can't pile up unnoticed. The tool keeps its own rules and configuration, so its findings match a run outside the portal; the portal adds one level, clean, and a ratchet that blocks new findings while existing ones are paid down.

no-findings.fix: Fix ruff's findings (the record's command reruns them), or, for a deliberate style, ignore the rule for those files under `[lint.per-file-ignores]` in ruff.toml with a comment saying why. A `# noqa` comment doesn't help: the check runs with --ignore-noqa.
no-findings.rationale: Each finding is a defect or a risk as the tool's authors define it, and it is cheapest to fix in the change that introduces it, while its author still has the context.

maintainer-python.title: Python we maintain passes ruff

maintainer-repo.description: The repository's level: the lowest level among its constituent scorecards, so one weak area holds the whole repository back (D86, docs/design/repo-level.md).
maintainer-repo.rationale: An average hides the weakest area, which is where the trouble is, so each level requires every counted scorecard to reach it, and the lowest names the one to raise next. Scorecards that need the CI runner are left out, so that a tool skipped on a laptop doesn't drop the repository to none.

constituents-at-least-bronze.fix: The repository level is the lowest constituent scorecard. Raise each one in the evidence to bronze.
constituents-at-least-bronze.rationale: One area below its floor is a weakness an average would hide, so the repository can't claim bronze until every counted scorecard reaches it.

constituents-at-least-gold.fix: Raise each constituent in the evidence to gold.
constituents-at-least-gold.rationale: Gold claims the top level in every counted area, so a single scorecard short of gold holds the repository back and is named as the next step.

constituents-at-least-silver.fix: Raise each constituent in the evidence to silver. A card whose highest level is bronze caps the repository at bronze.
constituents-at-least-silver.rationale: A repository called silver should be silver in every counted area, not on average; a lagging scorecard is exactly what the level exposes.

maintainer-repo.title: Repository level

maintainer-schema.description: Each JSON Schema compiled into the binary: Draft 2020-12 with an $id, titled and described, wired into the binary, with local $refs only and no credentials (D77).
maintainer-schema.rationale: These documents are the configuration and protocol contracts the binary enforces, and it compiles them as Draft 2020-12 without fetching remote references. A document that departs from that, or that nothing loads, looks like a contract but is not the one the server runs. Bronze is a valid, identifiable schema; silver ties it to the code; gold keeps it self-contained.

described.fix: Add a root `description` saying which contract this document is. Readers and agents meet the schema before the code.
described.rationale: Without a root description a reader has to work out which contract the document is from the code that loads it.

draft-2020-12.fix: Set $schema to https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema. The binary compiles schemas as that draft and no other.
draft-2020-12.rationale: Keywords from another dialect are read with 2020-12 meaning or ignored, so the server would validate differently from what the author wrote.

has-id.fix: Set $id to an absolute https URI. That is the schema's canonical identity in JSON Schema 2020-12.
has-id.rationale: The $id is the base URI that references resolve against and the name other tools cite. Without an absolute one the contract has no stable identity.

local-refs.fix: Point $ref at a fragment in this file. The compiler embeds the document and does not fetch a remote schema.
local-refs.rationale: A remote $ref cannot be resolved where the contract runs, and its target can change without a review in this repository.

no-hardcoded-secrets.fix: Remove the credential in the evidence. A schema is compiled into the binary and published with the repository.
no-hardcoded-secrets.rationale: A credential in a schema ships inside every build of the binary, where it cannot be removed without a new release.

titled.fix: Add a root `title`. JSON Schema defines it as the short name of the document.
titled.rationale: Editors and generated docs show the title as the schema's name. Without one, readers see only a file path or a URI.

wired-in.fix: Compile the document from crates/toolbox-model/src/schema.rs, or apply it from the reference portal validator. A schema file nothing loads is not a contract.
wired-in.rationale: A schema nothing compiles is never enforced, so it can drift from the real contract while still looking authoritative to readers and agents.

maintainer-schema.title: JSON Schemas

maintainer-site.description: Each public docs page: titled, described, linked, reachable from the sidebar, free of credentials, and not sharing its title (docs/design/site-standards.md).
maintainer-site.rationale: The site is what outside readers see of Toolbox, served from GitHub Pages, so an untitled page, a dead link or a leaked credential is a public defect. Bronze is a page that stands on its own; silver puts it where readers can find it; gold keeps pages distinguishable in search and navigation.

described.fix: Set `description:` in the page's frontmatter. It is the summary a reader and a search index see.
described.rationale: Without a description, search engines and link previews fall back to whatever text they scrape, and a reader cannot judge the page before opening it.

links-resolve.fix: Fix or remove the links in the evidence. A root-relative link must include the site base and name a content page, a file under site/public, or an Astro page under site/src/pages.
links-resolve.rationale: GitHub Pages serves the site under /toolbox and Starlight does not rewrite a link that already starts with /, so a link that misses the base or names no page is a 404 for every reader.

no-hardcoded-secrets.fix: Remove the credential in the evidence. A docs page is published to GitHub Pages.
no-hardcoded-secrets.rationale: A credential on a page is public as soon as the site deploys, and stays in the repository history after the page is fixed, so it has to be revoked.

reachable.fix: Add the page's directory to the sidebar `autogenerate` list in `site/astro.config.mjs`, or link its slug there. Leave `draft` unset.
reachable.rationale: The sidebar is how a reader of the site finds a page. One it does not list exists only for someone who already has the URL.

titled.fix: Set a top-level `title:` of at least 3 characters in the page's frontmatter. Starlight uses it as the page heading and the document title.
titled.rationale: An untitled page reaches readers, browser tabs and search results with no name, so nobody can recognise it before opening it.

unique-title.fix: Give the page a `title:` no other page in site/src/content/docs uses, so search results and the sidebar tell them apart.
unique-title.rationale: Two pages with one title look the same wherever titles are listed, so readers open the wrong one or assume one is a duplicate.

maintainer-site.title: Public docs pages

maintainer-skill.description: Each agent skill we ship: loadable, followable, honest about its limits and free of hidden instructions or credentials (D72, docs/design/skill-standards.md).
maintainer-skill.rationale: Skills are loaded into the prompts of operators' agents: an invalid or vague one is never used, and one carrying hidden text or a credential spreads it to every install. Bronze is what a harness needs to load and route a skill, plus those two safety items; silver is what an agent needs to follow it; gold adds stated limits, eval cases and a small bundle. Whether a skill raises task success needs paired model runs and is not gated.

description-says-when.fix: Say what the skill does and when to use it in the description (20 to 1024 characters), including when, whenever, before, or after.

links.title: Anthropic skill best practices (writing effective descriptions)

description-says-when.rationale: Only the name and description are loaded at startup, so the description alone decides whether a router picks the skill. Below 20 characters it cannot say when; above 1024 the spec rejects it.

has-evals.fix: Add at least three eval cases to evals/evals.json (a JSON array, or an object with an evals array). One element is one prompt. Running them is a separate, non-gating step.
has-evals.rationale: Without eval cases nobody can measure whether the skill helps or notice when an edit makes it worse. Three is Anthropic's bar for sharing; the cases are the contract a later paired-run job will execute.

has-example.fix: Add a fenced code block in SKILL.md with a concrete command, input, or output.
has-example.rationale: A concrete command or output shows the agent exactly what to run and what success looks like; a description alone invites a plausible but wrong invocation.

has-procedure.fix: Write at least three numbered steps in SKILL.md so an agent can follow the procedure.

links.title: Anthropic skill best practices (use workflows for complex tasks)

has-procedure.rationale: Prose without numbered steps leaves the order of work to the model, which can skip or reorder a step without noticing.

links-resolve.fix: Fix or remove the relative links in the evidence. Paths are relative to the file that contains them.
links-resolve.rationale: An agent follows a skill's links mid-task; a broken one sends it to a file that is not there, and it carries on without the detail the author moved out.

no-hardcoded-secrets.fix: Remove the hardcoded credentials in the evidence. Refer to a secret by name instead of pasting it into the skill.
no-hardcoded-secrets.rationale: A skill is published with its plugin and pasted into model prompts, so a credential in it reaches every install and every transcript. It sits at bronze so such a skill cannot pass the ratchet.

no-hidden-instructions.fix: Remove from the skill's files what a reader can't see and a model can: zero-width and other default-ignorable characters, bidi controls, variation selectors outside emoji, Unicode tags, HTML comments (`<!-- -->`) and Markdown link-reference comments (`[//]: # (...)`); save any non-UTF-8 text file as UTF-8 or remove it. Images, fonts and archives are not scanned.

links.title: Thresholds: why hidden text sits at bronze

no-hidden-instructions.rationale: A model reads characters and comments that a reviewer cannot see, so hidden text is a way to slip instructions past review. It sits at bronze, the lowest level, so such a skill cannot pass the ratchet.

one-level-deep.fix: Keep references one hop from SKILL.md and the skill to at most three supporting files. Focused skills outperform large bundles.
one-level-deep.rationale: Agents read deeply nested references only in part, so detail two hops away is easily missed. SkillsBench found focused skills with at most three modules beat larger bundles.

portable-paths.fix: Replace the Windows paths in the evidence with forward-slash paths relative to the skill directory.

links.title: Anthropic skill best practices (avoid Windows-style paths)

portable-paths.rationale: Skills are installed on macOS and Linux as well as Windows; a backslash path does not resolve there, so the agent cannot open the file it was told to read.

states-boundaries.fix: Name a limit, an error path, or a prerequisite in the body of `SKILL.md` (never, do not, limitation, prerequisite, troubleshooting, or on error).
states-boundaries.rationale: A skill that names no limit, prerequisite or error path leaves the agent to push on when a step fails, or to use the skill where it does not apply.

third-person.fix: Rewrite the description in third person. Drop you, your, I, we, my, and our; the description is loaded into the agent's prompt.
third-person.rationale: The description is injected into the agent's system prompt beside every other skill's, and a first- or second-person voice there blurs who is speaking and can hurt discovery.

valid-frontmatter.fix: Fix the Agent Skills frontmatter errors in the evidence (name, description, directory match, allowed fields).
valid-frontmatter.rationale: A harness that cannot parse the frontmatter, or finds a name that does not match the directory, does not load the skill, so every later rule is moot.

within-body-budget.fix: Keep the SKILL.md body under 500 lines and about 5000 tokens (characters divided by 4). Move detail into references/.
within-body-budget.rationale: The whole body enters the context window when the skill is selected, crowding out the task. The spec's guidance is under 500 lines and about 5000 tokens; tokens here are estimated as characters divided by 4.

maintainer-skill.title: Agent skills

maintainer-supply-chain.description: The repository files that turn on GitHub Advanced Security and dependency updates, beside what OpenSSF Scorecard carries (D85, D01M82E93XAPNE0WFXEPJZ59WG4).
maintainer-supply-chain.rationale: Dependency updates, owned workflows and pinned code scanning are switched on by files in the checkout, so they can be scored without the GitHub API, beside the checks OpenSSF Scorecard already carries. Bronze keeps every ecosystem updated, silver puts an owner on workflow changes, and gold pins the code-scanning action like any other.

code-scanning-pinned.fix: Pin github/codeql-action to a 40-character commit, the same way other actions are pinned.
code-scanning-pinned.rationale: The code-scanning action runs with the repository's token like any other action, so an unpinned one can be swapped under its tag. It stays until Scorecard's Pinned-Dependencies reaches 10 here and covers it.

dependabot.fix: Add .github/dependabot.yml updates for the ecosystems in the evidence (cargo, npm, github-actions).
dependabot.rationale: An ecosystem Dependabot doesn't cover gets no pull requests for new releases or security fixes, so its dependencies age unnoticed. Scorecard's Dependency-Update-Tool only asks that a tool exists, not that it covers each ecosystem.

workflows-have-owners.fix: Add a CODEOWNERS rule that covers .github/workflows (a catch-all * does). Workflow changes should have an owner.
workflows-have-owners.rationale: A workflow change can alter what runs with the repository's token and secrets, so it should reach a named owner for review; CODEOWNERS is how GitHub requests that review.

maintainer-supply-chain.title: Supply-chain security settings

meta-assessment.description: What every assessment must contain to be worth reading: a named assessor, suggestions for findings and citations that resolve in the repository (D80).
meta-assessment.rationale: Agents act on assessments and review cards read them, so a malformed one misleads twice: a finding without a suggestion can't be acted on, and a reason without a citation can't be checked. Bronze is the ratcheted floor every new assessment must meet; silver and gold ask for citations, first on findings, then on every verdict.

assessor-named.fix: Set `assessor.name` to the agent harness or person who made the assessment.
assessor-named.rationale: An unnamed assessment can't be weighed or challenged, and review-assessment needs the name to tell an independent review from a self-review.

cites-everything.fix: Cite a source in every listed reason, passes included, in the same forms as cites-for-findings (a path, a unique file name, an existing decision or question id, a URL), so a reviewer can check the verdict.
cites-everything.rationale: A pass is a claim too; without a citation a reviewer can't tell a checked pass from a guess, and a wrong pass hides a problem the assessment was meant to find.

cites-for-findings.check: entity.uncited.filter(c, c in entity.failing || c in entity.unsure).size() == 0
cites-for-findings.fix: In the assessment file under portal/assessments/, cite what each listed fail or unsure reason rests on, in a form a reader can open: a repository path (`crates/x/src/lib.rs:40`), a file name only one file has, a decision or question id that exists (D71, Q10), or a full URL. A section sign or a bare number alone isn't checkable.
cites-for-findings.rationale: A finding that cites nothing a reader can open can be neither verified nor disputed; on the first run, 6 of 9 assessments fell below silver because their reasons named a behaviour without a path or a number.

suggests-fixes.fix: Add a `suggestion:` to each listed fail or unsure verdict: the change that would make it pass.
suggests-fixes.rationale: A fail or unsure verdict with no suggested change leaves the reader to rediscover the fix, so the finding tends to go unacted.

meta-assessment.title: Assessments are well-formed

meta-connector.description: Each connector a portal configures: every record mapped, fixtures for tests, freshness declared and refresh by id (docs/design/scorecards-for-scorecards.md §5).
meta-connector.rationale: Every fact enters the portal through a connector, so its gaps become the portal's: unmapped records are lost, untested mappings break on live data, and stale data reads as current. The starter shipped without freshness or refresh, which pilots copying it would have inherited; a mapping and fixtures are the floor, freshness and refresh sit above it.

freshness-declared.fix: Declare `freshness:` for each listed record kind, so stale data shows as stale rather than current.
freshness-declared.rationale: With no freshness bound, data from a connector that stopped syncing reads as current, and rules pass or fail on stale facts.

has-fixtures.fix: Add fixtures/<connector>.ndjson with representative records, so tests run without the live system.
has-fixtures.rationale: Without fixture records, the connector's mappings run only against the live system, so tests and CI never exercise them.

records-mapped.fix: Map each listed record kind to a kind (`map: - from: <connector>/<record>`), or stop declaring it.
records-mapped.rationale: Records of a kind no map rule reads never become entities, so the portal silently lacks those facts while the connector appears to cover them.

refreshable.fix: Support refresh by external id for each listed record kind, so an agent can see its fix land.
refreshable.rationale: An agent that fixes something needs to refresh that one entity to see the rule pass; without refresh by id it waits for a full sync, or can't confirm the fix at all.

meta-connector.title: Portal connectors are well-formed

meta-field.description: Each field: populated in the fixtures, described and given a shape, so CEL, validation and agents know what it holds (docs/design/scorecards-for-scorecards.md §5).
meta-field.rationale: Fields are what rules, evidence and agents read: one never populated in fixtures has an untested mapping, an undescribed one is guessed at, and an opaque object can't be type-checked or validated. A value in some fixture is the floor for a new field; a description and a declared shape sit above it.

computed-readable.fix: Split the field's `computed:` expression into simpler fields and rules, or move the logic into the connector, so it reads at a glance.
computed-readable.rationale: A long or doubly nested computed field is hard to review and costs more on every entity. Computed fields get twice a check's budget because they are where logic belongs.

described.fix: Add a `description:` to the field: what it means, its unit, and where it comes from.
described.rationale: A field's meaning, unit and source aren't visible from its name, and a rule written against a misread field measures the wrong thing.

has-shape.fix: Replace the object with typed fields (or a list of strings), so CEL, validation and agents know its shape.
has-shape.rationale: With no declared shape, validation and CEL type checks can't see inside the object, so a renamed or missing key surfaces only as a wrong outcome in the rules that read it.

populated-in-fixtures.fix: Give at least one fixture record a value for the field, so its mapping (or computation) is exercised.
populated-in-fixtures.rationale: A field no fixture sets has a mapping or computation that no test runs, so it can be empty or wrong on every entity without anyone noticing.

meta-field.title: Fields are well-formed

meta-kind.description: Each kind of entity: in the fixtures, tested and described with every field, since every rule reads it (docs/design/scorecards-for-scorecards.md §5).
meta-kind.rationale: Every rule reads a kind, so a kind absent from fixtures and tests leaves its map rules and computed fields unexercised, and an undescribed one leaves agents guessing what an entity is. Being exercised in tests is the floor for a new kind; descriptions sit above it because they help readers without making any score wrong.

described.fix: Give the kind a `description:` saying what one entity is; agents read it before any field.
described.rationale: Agents read a kind's description before its fields. Without one, they infer what an entity is from field names and can act on the wrong thing.

fields-described.fix: Give each listed field a `description:`: what it means, its unit, and where it comes from.
fields-described.rationale: An undescribed field leaves its meaning, unit and origin to guesswork, and every rule and agent that reads it inherits the guess; 16 kinds had undescribed fields on the first run.

in-fixtures.fix: Add fixture records that map to the kind, so its map rules and computed fields run in tests.
in-fixtures.rationale: A kind with no fixture entities never runs its map rules or computed fields in tests, so a mapping error first shows on live data.

tested.fix: Add a test expectation about one of the kind's fixture entities (a field, a relation or a score).
tested.rationale: Fixture entities no expectation reads can change without any test failing; one expectation pins the kind's mapping. Three kinds were in no test on the first run.

meta-kind.title: Kinds are well-formed

meta-rubric.description: Each rubric agents judge with: described, used, guided with what counts as fail, and shown to discriminate on real assessments (D80).
meta-rubric.rationale: A rubric decides what agents judge, so a vague one yields reviews that disagree or pass everything. Described and used once is the floor for a new rubric; guidance on what counts as fail lets assessors agree; gold needs three assessments to show that each criterion can fail.

described.fix: Describe what the rubric judges and which sources the assessor should read.
described.rationale: The assessor reads the description to learn what to judge and which sources to read; without it, two assessors judge different things.

discriminates.fix: Sharpen or drop a criterion that everything passes; a question nothing fails asks nothing.
discriminates.rationale: A criterion every assessment passes costs assessor effort and tells nothing apart: `rule-quality`'s `fix-leads-to-pass` passed all four of its first rule assessments.

guided.fix: Give each listed criterion `guidance:` saying what counts as fail, so assessors agree.
guided.rationale: Without guidance on what counts as fail, assessors draw the line in different places and their verdicts can't be compared. Blank guidance used to pass (D01M831P5QWJQ4A2FT85N5MXJQF).

in-use.fix: Assess one entity with it (`toolbox assess brief <id> --rubric <name>`), or remove the rubric.
in-use.rationale: A rubric no assessment has used is untried configuration: nobody knows whether its questions can be answered from the sources it names.

meta-rubric.title: Rubrics are well-formed

meta-rule.description: Whether each rule is built properly: explained, tested, seen both passing and failing on fixtures, with evidence and a readable check. Gold here means well-formed, not good; whether a rule is good is the agents' review, Rules, reviewed by agents (D71, D01M831P5QWJQ4A2FT85N5MXJQF).
meta-rule.rationale: Every score in the portal is only as trustworthy as the rule behind it, and an untested or unexplained rule can pass everything, or fail for the wrong reason, unnoticed. Bronze is the floor every new rule must meet (tested, explained, decided on fixtures); silver adds both outcomes, evidence and a cost bound; gold asks for tests that pin both outcomes and for evidence and a fix that lead an agent to the change.

always-explains.fix: Add `evidence:` even for simple checks: it is what an agent reads first.
always-explains.rationale: Without evidence, an agent needed one `explain` call per rule per entity to find what failed; evidence shown with the fix removed that step (lesson L2, D66).

both-outcomes-on-fixtures.fix: Give the fixtures one entity that passes and one that fails, so both paths (and the evidence) are exercised.
both-outcomes-on-fixtures.rationale: A rule seen only passing may pass everything, and one seen only failing may fail everything; only both outcomes show it separates entities and that its evidence reads.

decided-on-fixtures.fix: Add fixture records the rule applies to, so it evaluates in tests.
decided-on-fixtures.rationale: A rule that is unknown on every fixture never runs its check in tests, so an error in its CEL first shows on real data, as `join` and `flatten` did twice (lesson L5).

evidence-tracks-check.fix: Write `evidence:` from what the check reads (the failing list itself, or the value compared), so it names what failed on this entity.
evidence-tracks-check.rationale: A fixed sentence says that a rule failed, not what failed on this entity, so the reader must redo the check. Agents fixed what the evidence named (lessons L1 and L2).

explains-fix.fix: Write a fix an agent can act on: what to change, and where.
explains-fix.rationale: A failing rule without a usable fix leaves the reader to reverse-engineer the check. A fresh agent raised a scorecard to gold using only fix texts that said what and where (lesson L1).

explains-why.fix: Give the rule a `rationale:` saying why it exists (the risk or the cost it guards against), and put the long story under `links:`.
explains-why.rationale: A reader who sees a failing rule needs to know why it matters before deciding to act, and a reviewer can't tell whether a check is a proxy without its goal. Links carry the long story, so the portal doesn't become an encyclopedia.

fix-names-a-place.fix: Say in `fix:` where to act: the file or directory (a path), the field the check reads, a `toolbox` command, or "the listed …" items of an evidence that names them (scorecards-for-scorecards.md, lesson L1).
fix-names-a-place.rationale: A fix that says what but not where sends an agent searching, which is where it guesses wrong. Fixes that named the file and field were what let a fresh agent raise a scorecard on its own (lesson L1).

no-nested-loops.fix: Avoid a comprehension inside a comprehension: compute the inner list in the connector or a computed field.
no-nested-loops.rationale: Rules are evaluated once per entity, so a loop inside a loop multiplies cost with the data; the 100k-entity budget already fails on 2-vCPU runners (lesson L8).

pins-both-outcomes.fix: In the portal's tests (tests/*.test.yaml), add an expectation that the rule passes for one fixture entity (`score('<card>', '<entity>').rules['<rule>'] == 'pass'`) and one that it fails for another (`== 'fail'`, or its evidence compared), so a change that flips either outcome is caught (lesson L4).
pins-both-outcomes.rationale: A rule whose tests pin only failing can start passing everything, and the tests still pass (lesson L4). Pinning both outcomes catches a change in either direction.

readable.fix: Move logic into a computed field or the connector, and keep the rule a short comparison.
readable.rationale: A long check hides its logic from the reader deciding whether a failure is fair, and costs more per entity. Logic in a computed field or the connector can be named and tested on its own.

tested.fix: In the portal's tests (tests/*.test.yaml), add an expectation that pins the rule: `score('<card>', '<entity>').rules['<rule>'] == 'fail'`, or its evidence compared (`.evidence['<rule>'] == [...]`). A bare mention doesn't count.
tested.rationale: An untested rule can change outcome after an edit with nothing to catch it. The first rules here gave false positives on a numbered Sources heading and a quoted "SDLC" (lesson L4).

meta-rule.title: Rules are well-formed

meta-scorecard.description: Each scorecard's form: described, tested, no empty level, fixtures that climb the ladder to every level. Gold means well-formed, not good (D71, D01M831P5QWJQ4A2FT85N5MXJQF).
meta-scorecard.rationale: A scorecard is the ladder readers climb, so its levels must exist and be exercised: an empty level is granted for nothing, and a level no fixture reaches has never been seen to work. Bronze, tested with no empty level, is the floor for every new scorecard; silver adds a description, a reason, a fixture ladder and tested rules; gold has a fixture at every level.

described.fix: Give the scorecard a `description:` saying what the standard covers; agents read it before any rule.
described.rationale: Agents read a scorecard's description before its rules. Without one, they infer the standard's purpose from its checks and may work towards the wrong goal.

every-level-has-rules.fix: Give every level at least one rule, or drop the level.
every-level-has-rules.rationale: A level with no rules is granted to every entity that reaches the one below it, so it tells the reader nothing about the entities at it.

every-rule-tested.fix: Add an expectation for each untested rule.
every-rule-tested.rationale: One untested rule is enough for a scorecard's levels to drift. A rule without a test was the most common scorecard gap on the first run, in 11 scorecards.

explains-why.fix: Give the scorecard a `rationale:` saying why the standard exists and why its levels are where they are, with `links:` to the decision or design behind it.
explains-why.rationale: A description says what a standard covers, not why anyone should meet it. Without the risk and the reason for its levels, a reader can't weigh a failure before acting, and links keep that long story out of the portal so it doesn't become an encyclopedia.

fixtures-reach-every-level.fix: Add fixture entities that reach each listed level, so every rung of the ladder is exercised in tests (portal/fixtures/).
fixtures-reach-every-level.rationale: A level no fixture reaches is untested: its rules may never pass together, and nothing shows that an entity can reach it (lesson L12).

fixtures-show-the-ladder.fix: Give the scorecard fixtures at two outcomes, one of them a real level: one entity at none and one at bronze or above, or two at different levels. Skipped entities show no ladder.
fixtures-show-the-ladder.rationale: Fixtures at one outcome never show the scorecard telling a better entity from a worse one. A ladder of `none` and `skipped` used to pass, so one real level is now required (D01M831P5QWJQ4A2FT85N5MXJQF).

tested.fix: Add at least one expectation for the scorecard in the portal's tests.
tested.rationale: A scorecard no expectation names can change its levels or lose a rule with no test noticing; on the first run, `user-cli` had no test of any kind.

meta-scorecard.title: Scorecards are well-formed

operator-cli.description: Each CLI command an operator runs on a portal: documented, with help for every argument and exercised by a test, so an agent can use it without reading the source (operator SDLC).
operator-cli.rationale: Operators' agents run these commands at every step of changing a portal, and they learn a command from its help and the docs, not from the Rust source. Bronze means an agent can find and read about the command; silver means it can use every flag and a test fails when the command breaks.

args-described.fix: Add a /// doc comment to each argument in the evidence.
args-described.rationale: An undescribed flag leaves an agent to guess its format and default from its name; a wrong guess is a failed run or a quietly different result.

documented.fix: Describe `toolbox <command>` in docs/v1-spec.md §7.7 or the operator SDLC doc.
documented.rationale: Help is read only by someone who already knows the command exists. An agent planning a change finds commands in the docs, so an undocumented command goes unused.

exercised.fix: Run the command in an acceptance script (`scripts/m*-acceptance.sh`) or an integration test under `crates/toolbox-cli/tests/`.
exercised.rationale: A command that no script or test runs can break without CI noticing, and an operator finds out halfway through a change to their portal.

has-help.fix: Give the command's variant in `crates/toolbox-cli/src/main.rs` a `///` doc comment; clap shows it as the command's help.
has-help.rationale: `--help` is the first thing an agent runs on an unfamiliar command; without help text it has to guess what the command does or read the source.

operator-cli.title: Operator CLI commands

review-assessment.description: Each assessment reviewed against assessment-quality by another assessor, advisory; reviews of reviews are not made (D80, D01M831P5QWJQ4A2FT85N5MXJQF).
review-assessment.rationale: A deterministic check sees that an assessment cites something, not that the source says what the reason claims; a second assessor's review checks that. Reviews stop at one level, so assessments made with assessment-quality are skipped, and the card is advisory because a review goes stale on every edit.

assessed.fix: Run `toolbox assess brief <assessment id> --portal portal`; a different agent or person should review it.
assessed.rationale: A review by the assessment's own assessor repeats its blind spots and is no independent check; one of the first three assessment reviews was a self-review.

no-doubts.fix: Resolve what the reviewer was unsure of, usually by citing the source a verdict rests on.
no-doubts.rationale: A reviewer's doubt usually means a verdict rests on taste rather than a cited source, so a second assessor reading the same sources might reach a different one.

no-open-findings.fix: A current assessment-quality assessment failed the listed criteria: act on its suggestions (portal/assessments/), then re-assess. If the finding is wrong, say why in a new assessment by another assessor.
no-open-findings.rationale: Failing reviews were lost among the unreviewed lines and went unacted for days; putting the assessment at none makes an open finding head the report until it is fixed or disputed.

passes-review.fix: For a listed criterion, revise the assessment file in portal/assessments/ where the review found it unsupported or incomplete, then have it reviewed again. For an item marked "fix the review", the review file is at fault: its reasons must cite what they rest on, including this assessment's file or the sources it cites.
passes-review.rationale: Gold means an independent reviewer checked the assessment against its own sources and found it sound; a review that cites only unrelated files can't have checked it.

review-assessment.title: Assessments, reviewed
