review-crate.description: An agent reviews each crate's design: no open finding is bronze, a current review is silver, and a clean review that a second agent checked is gold. Any change to the crate's code makes its review stale, and the card advises rather than gates (D79, D01M831P5QWJQ4A2FT85N5MXJQF).
review-crate.rationale: Deterministic rules measure a crate's form; whether it is well designed for its place takes judgement, so agents assess it against crate-design. Open findings come first at bronze, silver needs a review of the current sources, and gold a passing, grounded review checked by a second assessor. It is advisory, because a review that goes stale on every change must not gate the ratchet.

assessed.fix: Have an agent review the crate's current sources: `toolbox assess brief crate:<name> --portal portal` names the assessment file to write, and `toolbox assess check portal` checks it.
assessed.rationale: A review's verdict holds for the sources it read; once src/, tests/ or Cargo.toml change it may no longer be true, so only a review of the current hash counts.

independently-reviewed.fix: Have another agent or person review the crate-design assessment: `toolbox assess brief assessment:crate-design/crate:<name> --portal portal`, with reasons that cite the assessment file or the sources it cites; act on what that review fails.
independently-reviewed.rationale: An assessor reviewing its own assessment tends to confirm it, and when this rule was added one of three assessment reviews was self-review. A second assessor's grounded review makes the verdict more than one agent's opinion.

no-doubts.fix: Resolve what the assessor was unsure of (cite the source the verdict needs, in portal/assessments/), then re-assess with `toolbox assess brief crate:<name> --portal portal`. An open question in docs/questions.md doesn't pass this rule by itself.
no-doubts.rationale: An unsure verdict is an unanswered question about the design; at gold it must be settled with a source, not left as a doubt that reads like a pass.

no-open-findings.fix: A current crate-design assessment failed the listed criteria: act on its suggestions (portal/assessments/), then re-assess. If the finding is wrong, say why in a new assessment by another assessor.
no-open-findings.rationale: A failing criterion is a design problem someone has already found, and findings left unacted make review a formality. A stale review's findings still count until a new assessment closes them.

passes-review.fix: Act on the failing criteria's suggestions in the assessment (portal/assessments/), then re-assess.
passes-review.rationale: Gold claims the design holds up under review, so the current review must pass every criterion with reasons that cite something real: a reason that cites nothing can't be checked by anyone else.

review-crate.title: Crates, reviewed by agents

review-rule.description: Agents' judgement of each rule against rule-quality, advisory: an open finding is none, a current review is silver, a clean, cited one with no doubts is gold (D79, D01M831P5QWJQ4A2FT85N5MXJQF).
review-rule.rationale: Form checks can't tell whether a rule measures its intent or can be gamed: of 19 rules and scorecards that reached gold on the form checks and that agents reviewed, none passed. Open findings rank lowest so they head the report; the card is advisory because a review goes stale whenever its subject changes, and gating on it would block every edit.

assessed.fix: Run `toolbox assess brief <rule id> --portal portal`, have your agent write the assessment file it names, then `toolbox assess check portal`.
assessed.rationale: Without a current review, nobody has judged whether the rule as it now stands measures its intent; a verdict on an earlier version may not apply to the check.

no-doubts.fix: Resolve what the assessor was unsure of: usually a missing source for a threshold or an unstated intent.
no-doubts.rationale: An unsure verdict usually marks a threshold with no source or an intent nobody wrote down, which is where a rule drifts into a proxy (lesson L9).

no-open-findings.fix: A current rule-quality assessment failed the listed criteria: act on its suggestions (portal/assessments/), then re-assess. If the finding is wrong, say why in a new assessment by another assessor.
no-open-findings.rationale: A failing review names a way the rule misleads or can be gamed. Two such findings sat unacted for three days, buried among unreviewed rules, so an open finding now drops the rule to none.

passes-review.fix: Act on the failing criteria's suggestions in the assessment (portal/assessments/), then re-assess.
passes-review.rationale: A review that fails a criterion found a problem, and one whose reasons cite nothing that resolves can't be checked; either way the rule isn't known to be good.

review-rule.title: Rules, reviewed by agents

review-scorecard.description: An agent reviews whether each scorecard measures one concern and climbs a real ladder: no open finding is bronze, a current review is silver, and a clean, cited one with no doubts is gold. The card advises rather than gates (D79, D01M831P5QWJQ4A2FT85N5MXJQF).
review-scorecard.rationale: Form checks can't tell whether a scorecard measures one concern, climbs a real ladder or leaves an obvious gap; an adversarial review failed every scorecard it sampled that had reached gold on the form checks. The ladder and advisory status match review-rule: open findings first, and never gating, because a review goes stale when the scorecard changes.

assessed.fix: Run `toolbox assess brief <scorecard id> --portal portal`, have your agent write the assessment file it names, then `toolbox assess check portal`.
assessed.rationale: A review is tied to the scorecard's content hash; once the scorecard changes, the old verdict may no longer describe its rules or levels.

no-doubts.fix: Resolve what the assessor was unsure of: usually a level whose purpose isn't written down.
no-doubts.rationale: An unsure verdict usually marks a level whose purpose nobody wrote down, and a level nobody can justify is one readers can't trust.

no-open-findings.fix: A current scorecard-quality assessment failed the listed criteria: act on its suggestions (portal/assessments/), then re-assess. If the finding is wrong, say why in a new assessment by another assessor.
no-open-findings.rationale: A failing review names a gap or a broken ladder that every entity the scorecard scores inherits; dropping the scorecard to none keeps the finding at the top of the report until someone acts on it.

passes-review.fix: Act on the failing criteria's suggestions in the assessment (portal/assessments/), then re-assess.
passes-review.rationale: A review that fails a criterion found a problem, and one whose reasons cite nothing that resolves can't be checked; either way the scorecard isn't known to be good.

review-scorecard.title: Scorecards, reviewed by agents

review-sdlc-stage.description: An agent reviews whether each SDLC stage does what it claims: an open finding is none, a current review is silver, and a clean, cited one is gold. The card advises rather than gates (D79, D01M831P5QWJQ4A2FT85N5MXJQF).
review-sdlc-stage.rationale: The sdlc-stage card sees that a stage is declared and gated, not whether an agent can carry it out with released artifacts and without changing Toolbox's core; only judgement answers that. It is advisory because a review goes stale whenever the stage changes, and an open finding drops the stage to none so it is acted on, not buried.

assessed.fix: Run `toolbox assess brief sdlc-stage:<layer>/<stage> --portal portal`, have your agent write the assessment, then `toolbox assess check portal`.
assessed.rationale: A review of an older version judges a stage that no longer exists; only a review of the current declaration says anything about the stage as written.

no-doubts.fix: Resolve what the assessor was unsure of, usually a missing measurement or an unstated exit criterion.
no-doubts.rationale: An unsure verdict means the stage's own sources could not settle a criterion; a stage an agent is meant to carry out alone has to be clear enough for a reviewer to decide.

no-open-findings.fix: A current sdlc-stage-quality assessment failed the listed criteria: act on its suggestions (portal/assessments/), then re-assess. If the finding is wrong, say why in a new assessment by another assessor.
no-open-findings.rationale: Failing reviews were lost among the not-assessed lines and went unacted for days; putting the stage at none makes an open finding head the report until it is fixed or disputed.

passes-review.fix: Act on the failing criteria's suggestions in the assessment (portal/assessments/), then re-assess.
passes-review.rationale: Gold means a reviewer found the stage sound and every reason cites something that resolves, so the verdict can be checked rather than taken on trust.

review-sdlc-stage.title: SDLC stages, reviewed by agents

sdlc-layer.description: Each SDLC layer as a whole: every stage declared, none missing in fact, and all built (D87, docs/sdlc.md).
sdlc-layer.rationale: A layer can score well stage by stage while a whole stage is missing, as most of the package author SDLC still is. Scoring the layer exposes the hole: bronze when every stage is declared, silver when every stage is at least designed, gold when the whole loop is built.

every-stage-built.fix: Raise each listed stage to built (see sdlc-stage for what each lacks).
every-stage-built.rationale: A layer serves its builders only when they can run the whole plan, build, test, deploy and monitor loop; one stage left unbuilt breaks that loop for everyone in the layer.

nothing-missing.fix: For each listed stage in portal/sdlc/stages/<layer>.yaml, write the design (a doc, or a section of one, that names the stage), point `docs:` at it, then set `status:` to designed, partial or built. A status alone doesn't count, nor does a listed doc that is missing or never names the stage.
nothing-missing.rationale: A status is the author's own claim. Requiring a listed doc that exists and names the stage means a layer can't call a stage designed on the author's word alone; whether that doc really designs the stage is left to review.

stages-declared.fix: Declare each listed stage in portal/sdlc/stages/<layer>.yaml, even if its status is missing.
stages-declared.rationale: An undeclared stage is invisible to every other rule, so a layer could reach gold while skipping it; declaring it, even as missing, puts the gap on the report.

sdlc-layer.title: SDLC layers

sdlc-stage.description: Each stage of an SDLC layer, checked against facts: an exit criterion, a doc that exists, commands that resolve, checks CI runs, and status built (D87, docs/sdlc.md).
sdlc-stage.rationale: A layer's loop holds only if each stage has a gate an agent can run; a stage that exists only in prose leaves agents guessing when they are done. The levels climb from declared and documented, to runnable by an agent and verified in CI, to built with no open gaps.

agent-operable.fix: List under `commands:` a command that carries out the stage: a known tool (toolbox, cargo, npm, python3 …) or a script that exists in the repository. Fix or remove each listed command.
agent-operable.rationale: Agents do most of the work in every layer; a stage with no command, or one naming a script that was never written, needs a person to work out how to carry it out.

automated.fix: Add a CI step, acceptance script or test that proves the exit criterion, list it under `checks:`, and run each listed check from a workflow in .github/workflows.
automated.rationale: An exit criterion that no CI job runs is checked by eye, if at all, and regresses without anyone noticing; CI is what keeps it true after every change.

built.fix: Close the listed gaps, then set `status: built` and empty `gaps:`.
built.rationale: Gold is kept for stages that work today with nothing left open, so the report separates what agents can rely on from what is only designed or partly built.

documented.fix: Point `docs:` (and `checks:`) in portal/sdlc/stages/<layer>.yaml at files that exist; write the doc if it doesn't.
documented.rationale: A stage that points at a missing doc or check claims a design or a gate that isn't there, and an agent following the pointer reaches a dead end.

has-exit-criterion.fix: Write the exit criterion as something checkable: the command that passes, or the artifact that exists.
has-exit-criterion.rationale: Without an exit criterion no agent or person can tell when the stage is done; the maintainer SDLC works because every exit criterion can be proved without someone checking by eye.

status-known.fix: Set `status:` in portal/sdlc/stages/<layer>.yaml to built, partial, designed or missing.
status-known.rationale: sdlc-layer counts stages by status, and a value outside the four is never counted as missing, so a typo could hide a stage that doesn't exist yet.

sdlc-stage.title: SDLC stages

user-cli.description: Each CLI command a portal's users and their agents call: help, structured output and a test that runs it, so scripts can depend on it (user SDLC).
user-cli.rationale: Users' scripts, CI checks and apps call these commands and parse what they print, so an unannounced change breaks them. Bronze means a caller can find the command and parse its output; silver means every flag is explained and a test runs the command.

args-described.fix: Add a /// doc comment to each argument in the evidence.
args-described.rationale: An undescribed flag leaves an agent to guess its format and default from its name; a wrong guess is a failed run or a quietly different result.

exercised.fix: Run the command in an acceptance script (`scripts/m*-acceptance.sh`) or an integration test under `crates/toolbox-cli/tests/`.
exercised.rationale: Users' scripts depend on this command's behaviour; if no script or test runs it, a regression reaches them before CI sees it.

has-help.fix: Give the command's variant in `crates/toolbox-cli/src/main.rs` a `///` doc comment; clap shows it as the command's help.
has-help.rationale: `--help` is the first thing an agent runs on an unfamiliar command; without help text it has to guess what the command does or read the source.

structured-output.fix: Support `-o json` (or `--format json`) so scripts and apps can parse the output.
structured-output.rationale: A script that parses Markdown or table text breaks when the wording changes; JSON gives a CI check a shape it can depend on. `toolbox mcp` is exempt because it is a stdio bridge, not a read.

user-cli.title: User CLI commands

user-mcp.description: Each built-in MCP tool: described inputs and a contract test that calls it successfully, so agents can rely on its schema (user SDLC).
user-mcp.rationale: MCP tools are the contract users' agents and apps build on, and their names, inputs and result shapes may change only additively within a major version. Bronze means an agent can choose the tool and its client can tell a read from a write; silver means it can call the tool correctly; gold means a test calls it over MCP, because the first direct tests found bugs the CLI path did not show.

annotated.fix: Set annotations.readOnlyHint (and idempotent/openWorld hints for writes).
annotated.rationale: Toolbox leaves prompt-injection defence to the client's approval layer and owes it accurate annotations; without `readOnlyHint` a client cannot tell a safe read from a call that needs the user's approval.

contract-tested.fix: Call the tool directly (tools/call) in a test, e.g. crates/toolbox-api/tests; the CLI path in `viaCli` doesn't pin the MCP contract.
contract-tested.rationale: A tool reached only through the CLI leaves its MCP schema and `structuredContent` untested, and those are what users' agents read. A call that errors proves nothing, so when the runner observes the tests only successful calls count; the static read can only see that a test names the tool.

described.fix: Write the tool's `description` (at least 20 characters): what it returns and when an agent should call it.
described.rationale: An agent picks a tool from its `tools/list` description alone; a short or vague one means the right tool is skipped or the wrong one is called.

documented.fix: List the tool, in backticks, in docs/v1-spec.md §7.3.
documented.rationale: The v1 spec is the contract users build against, so a tool missing there carries no promise. Naming that file, not any doc, stops common names such as `get` passing on a stray mention.

inputs-described.fix: Add a description to each input property in the evidence (crates/toolbox-api/src/mcp.rs).
inputs-described.rationale: An agent fills a tool's inputs from the schema it is given; without descriptions it guesses formats and defaults. The fresh-agent run had to read the REST handlers to work out 15 of them.

user-mcp.title: MCP tools

vs-backstage-agent-surface.description: What a coding agent gets: MCP by default, and how many tokens it spends to learn the tools and read one entity.
vs-backstage-agent-surface.rationale: Coding agents are a primary audience of a portal, and every byte a tool returns is tokens they pay for and context the task loses. A portal without MCP leaves each adopter to build and secure their own agent integration.

get-entity-size.fix: Trim the get tool's response in crates/toolbox-api/src/mcp.rs to the fields an agent asks for.
get-entity-size.rationale: Reading an entity is an agent's routine call, so a bloated response multiplies its token cost and buries the fields it asked for.

mcp-by-default.fix: Serve /mcp from `toolbox serve` and stdio from `toolbox mcp`.
mcp-by-default.rationale: If MCP is an add-on, each adopter must install, configure and secure it before an agent can read the catalog. Both products serve it by default, so this rule is parity.

tools-list-size.fix: Shorten tool descriptions and schemas in crates/toolbox-api/src/mcp.rs.
tools-list-size.rationale: An agent loads tools/list before it does anything, so its size is a fixed token cost on every session and crowds out the task's context. Backstage is measured with its unrestricted MCP token.

vs-backstage-agent-surface.title: Agent surface

vs-backstage-capabilities.description: What a portal does out of the box, by configuration alone, and the community that keeps it going: 12 rules are features and one, community, counts contributors. The scenarios come from the Backstage parity audit, so they favour what Backstage ships.
vs-backstage-capabilities.rationale: Functional completeness is the first question in a portal evaluation: a team will not adopt a portal that lacks what its developers use every day. Toolbox is expected to lose here, and each missing capability is published as a loss rather than dropped.

api-docs.fix: Render an API entity's definition in the UI through a UI extension.
api-docs.rationale: A rendered API definition lets a consumer read a service's contract where they found the service; otherwise it sits unread in the provider's repository.

catalog-browse.fix: Keep the catalog pages in the UI and `toolbox query`.
catalog-browse.rationale: Browsing and filtering the catalog is a portal's base job; without it, people and agents cannot find a service or the team behind it.

community.fix: Make a first contribution easy: CONTRIBUTING.md, good first issues, and a green `cargo test` on a fresh clone.

links.title: Setting up a project for healthy contributions

community.rationale: Contributors fix bugs, review changes and keep a project alive when a maintainer leaves; with a handful, the adopter carries the risk that it stalls.

docs.fix: Carry each component's site, as its own documentation tool builds it, the way the box carries other tools' output.

links.title: The box and the tools it carries

docs.rationale: Without a component's docs in the portal, developers switch to a separate docs site, and the portal stops being the one place to learn about a service.

docs-search.fix: Index documentation text with the entities, so `toolbox search` finds answers inside documents as well as names and titles.
docs-search.rationale: Developers search for answers in documentation, not only for entity names; a portal whose search stops at names and titles sends them to another tool.

graph.rationale: Relations show what a change or an outage affects; without a graph, impact analysis means reading descriptors one by one.

kubernetes.fix: Add a connector that reads workloads from the Kubernetes API.
kubernetes.rationale: Seeing a component's workloads lets its owner check what runs where without cluster access; without it, on-call leaves the portal for kubectl at the first question.

mcp-read.rationale: Without MCP read tools, an agent cannot ask the portal who owns what, and guesses from code and commit history instead.

notifications.fix: Notify owners when a score or what they own changes, through a connector or a webhook.
notifications.rationale: Without notifications, a score drop or a change to what a team owns is noticed only when someone happens to open the portal.

ownership.fix: Keep `toolbox owner` and the owner_of MCP tool.
ownership.rationale: Incident response, reviews and access requests start from who owns a service; a portal that cannot answer through teams leaves people asking in chat.

permission-rule.fix: Keep the OpenFGA model in the manifest.
permission-rule.rationale: Organisations differ in who may see and do what; without custom rules, a portal's access model is too open or forked. Backstage's rule is TypeScript code, counted in its favour.

scorecards.fix: Keep scorecards in the manifest, as the v1 spec defines them.
scorecards.rationale: Scorecards turn standards into what each team must fix next; without them, standards live in documents nobody checks. Backstage passes through the Tech Insights add-on, configured in code.

templates.fix: Build self-service actions, the v1 milestone that runs them, once the decision that paused them is lifted.

links.title: How an action run would work

templates.rationale: Templates are how a platform spreads its defaults to new services; without them, each service starts as a copy of an old one. Toolbox's self-service actions are paused while their coordination is reviewed.

vs-backstage-capabilities.title: Capabilities

vs-backstage-change-safety.description: Changing a portal safely: validate before deploy, preview the effect, upgrade without merging, roll back without surgery. ISO 25010 maintainability; DORA change failure rate and recovery time.

links.title: Factor definitions: upgrade cost, analysability and recoverability

vs-backstage-change-safety.rationale: A portal's bad data and outages mostly arrive with a change: a config edit, a catalog edit or an upgrade. Checking and previewing a change before deploy lowers the change failure rate, and rolling back without database surgery shortens recovery (DORA).

change-preview.fix: Keep `toolbox plan --local --base <manifest>` diffing entities, scores and tuples.
change-preview.rationale: Without a preview, production is the first place a change shows that it re-owned entities, moved scores or widened access; a diff before deploy catches those in review.

offline-validate.fix: Keep `toolbox validate` and `toolbox test` working with no server or database.
offline-validate.rationale: If validation needs a running instance, CI and pre-commit checks need one too, so catalog mistakes surface after deploy. Backstage's catalog validate takes `--instance`.

rollback-steps.fix: Keep the store's migrations readable by the previous release, as experiments/backstage-compare/upgrade.py checks.
rollback-steps.rationale: A rollback that needs hand-run database steps is slow and error-prone in the incident that calls for it. Backstage documents a manual Knex `migrate:down`, run from the newer version.

upgrade-lines.fix: Keep examples/repo-portal-starter passing `toolbox validate` and `toolbox test` across releases (experiments/backstage-compare/upgrade.py).
upgrade-lines.rationale: Lines an adopter edits per release are a cost paid on every release for the portal's life, and adopters who skip it stay on unpatched releases. Unlike measures: Toolbox counts required lines, Backstage its suggested template diff.

vs-backstage-change-safety.title: Change safety

vs-backstage-extensibility.description: What it takes to add an integration: which languages, and whether the server is rebuilt. ISO 25010 modifiability.
vs-backstage-extensibility.rationale: Extensions are where portals accrete cost: an integration built into the core is rebuilt, redeployed and upgraded with it. A protocol any language can speak, added without a rebuild, keeps that cost with the integration's owner (Parnas). Not pre-registered on its own; the README counts it inside capabilities.

any-language.fix: Keep the connector protocol language-neutral, as schema/connector-messages.schema.json defines it.
any-language.rationale: If integrations must be written in the portal's own language and framework, the teams who own the data cannot write them, and the platform team becomes the bottleneck.

without-rebuild.fix: Keep remote connectors pushing to /v1/ingest with their own token (docs/design/connector-control.md).
without-rebuild.rationale: If adding an integration means rebuilding and redeploying the server, every new data source becomes a core release, with its risk and its wait in the platform team's queue.

vs-backstage-extensibility.title: Extensibility

vs-backstage-footprint.description: What it costs to run and to own: memory, disk, and the files an adopter keeps for a first portal.
vs-backstage-footprint.rationale: Memory, disk and the files an adopter keeps are paid for on every instance, preview environment and upgrade, and they decide the smallest machine and team that can run a portal. Toolbox promises a deployment of one container image plus Postgres; a heavy footprint would break that promise.

adopter-files.fix: Move what examples/repo-portal-starter asks an adopter to keep into packages they include.
adopter-files.rationale: Every file an adopter keeps is theirs to merge on each upgrade, so a portal that starts as a generated app makes the adopter its maintainer. Toolbox counts its repo starter; its served portal gives the same standing.

adopter-lines.fix: Move what examples/repo-portal-starter asks an adopter to keep into packages they include.
adopter-lines.rationale: Lines kept are lines someone must read, review and carry through every upgrade; they set how long a first portal takes to understand and how much can break when the product changes.

idle-memory.fix: Measure the server and its co-processes with experiments/backstage-compare/measure.py and trim what starts eagerly.
idle-memory.rationale: Idle memory is paid by every instance, replica and preview environment whether or not anyone reads it, and sets the smallest machine a portal can run on.

install-size.fix: Measure with experiments/backstage-compare/footprint.py and drop what the release archives carry but do not run.
install-size.rationale: Bytes on disk are pulled on every deploy, cold start and CI job, and every file shipped is one more thing to scan and patch.

loaded-memory.fix: Measure with experiments/backstage-compare/measure.py and shrink the derived state's copies in crates/toolbox-api/src/state.rs.
loaded-memory.rationale: Memory that grows with the catalog decides when an instance runs out as the organisation adds services; a portal that fits at 1k components can be killed for memory at 10k.

vs-backstage-footprint.title: Footprint

vs-backstage-org-fit.description: Fitting how an organisation is built: one repository with no server first, then many portals joined. Conway's law and Team Topologies.
vs-backstage-org-fit.rationale: Systems take the shape of the organisation that builds them (Conway), and teams move fastest when they can test without an integrated environment (DORA, loosely coupled teams). A portal that needs a central server first makes every team wait for the platform team; one that cannot join portals cannot grow past one.

federation.fix: Build federation as its design describes.

links.title: Decision: federation is designed, not built

federation.rationale: Without federation, a large organisation runs one catalog for everyone or many that never join, and neither fits teams that own their portals. Neither product federates, so this rule is parity.

repo-scoped.fix: Keep `toolbox report` scoring a repository with no server, as actions/report does.

links.title: Decision: the report as a GitHub Action

repo-scoped.rationale: A team that can score its own repository in CI, with no server, gets value before anyone runs a portal, and the platform team has nothing to operate for it.

vs-backstage-org-fit.title: Org fit

vs-backstage-performance.description: Start, read and recover on a 10k-component catalog, with every read authorized (Toolbox through OpenFGA, Backstage under allow-all). ISO 25010 performance efficiency and reliability.

links.title: Factor definitions: footprint, read latency, freshness and recovery

vs-backstage-performance.rationale: Every page load, agent call and CI job reads the portal, so a slow start, slow reads or a slow recovery cost all of its users at once. The pass thresholds were fixed before the run; Toolbox authorizes every read while Backstage runs allow-all, which favours Backstage.

catalog-readable.fix: Time ingest and recompute in `toolbox serve` logs and the derive laps, then rerun experiments/backstage-compare/run.sh.
catalog-readable.rationale: Until ingest finishes, the portal answers from a partial catalog, and people and agents read wrong owners and scores without knowing it. This covers the first ingest only, not later freshness.

get-latency.fix: Profile GET /v1/entities/{id} in crates/toolbox-api/src/routes.rs, then rerun experiments/backstage-compare/run.sh.
get-latency.rationale: An entity page fans out into many reads, so the per-call tail becomes the page's typical latency (Dean and Barroso, The Tail at Scale); a slow p95 makes every page and agent lookup slow.

get-throughput.fix: Profile GET /v1/entities/{id} in crates/toolbox-api/src/routes.rs, then rerun experiments/backstage-compare/run.sh.
get-throughput.rationale: Throughput decides how many people, agents and CI jobs one instance serves before it needs replicas. Toolbox's reads here are mostly authorization-cache hits, and the load shares the CPUs: a ceiling, not a capacity.

list-latency.fix: Profile the filtered list in crates/toolbox-api/src/routes.rs (list_entities), then rerun experiments/backstage-compare/run.sh.
list-latency.rationale: Filtered lists back the catalog filter, ownership views and the MCP query tool, so a slow filter slows every "what does this team own" question. Toolbox lost here in round 1, before the field index.

list-throughput.fix: Profile the filtered list in crates/toolbox-api/src/routes.rs (list_entities), then rerun experiments/backstage-compare/run.sh.
list-throughput.rationale: A filter that scans every entity gets slower as the catalog grows, so a portal that copes at 1k components stalls at 10k. Round 1's loss here, about 2.4× behind, is published as written.

ready.fix: Profile startup with `RUST_LOG=debug toolbox serve`, then rerun experiments/backstage-compare/run.sh.
ready.rationale: Start time bounds how soon a crashed or rescheduled instance, a preview environment or a scale-from-zero deploy serves again; a slow start turns each of those into an outage.

recovery.fix: Time the restart path in crates/toolbox-api/src/state.rs (the first recompute from Postgres), then rerun experiments/backstage-compare/run.sh.
recovery.rationale: After a crash the portal is down until its state is back, so recovery time adds to every incident (DORA failed deployment recovery time). A product whose state is derived should recover by recomputing.

vs-backstage-performance.title: Performance

vs-backstage-security.description: Secure by default, as installed: what an unauthenticated or forging client gets, what a client token can destroy, and what an extension can reach. ISO 25010 security.

links.title: Factor definitions: secure defaults and extension isolation

vs-backstage-security.rationale: A portal maps every service, its owners and how to reach them, and the configuration it ships with is often the one deployed. OWASP ASVS V13 asks that the default be secure for use on the Internet, so each rule probes the product as it ships, and a setting the adopter must remember to change counts as a fail.

anonymous-mcp.fix: Authenticate /mcp as the REST API does, in crates/toolbox-api/src/mcp.rs.
anonymous-mcp.rationale: MCP reads the same catalog as the API, so an unauthenticated MCP endpoint is a side door around every access rule the API enforces.

anonymous-read.fix: Refuse a read without credentials outside dev mode in crates/toolbox-authz/src/authn.rs.
anonymous-read.rationale: A catalog readable without credentials hands the organisation's service map, owners and internal links to anyone who can reach the port.

client-cannot-delete.fix: Keep entity writes to connectors' ingest; offer no DELETE in crates/toolbox-api/src/routes.rs.
client-cannot-delete.rationale: A read client's token ends up in scripts and agent configs; if it can delete entities, a leaked token becomes lost data. Backstage is scored on its read-only REST token; its MCP-capable token can still delete.

extension-credential-isolated.fix: Start connectors with a cleared environment and an allowlist, in crates/toolbox-api/src/connectors.rs.
extension-credential-isolated.rationale: An extension that holds the server's database or authorization credentials can read and rewrite everything, so one compromised integration is a compromised portal. Rescored to fail for both: a same-user connector read OpenFGA's memory on a host without Yama.

extension-process-isolated.fix: Run every connector as its own process, as docs/design/connector-control.md says.
extension-process-isolated.rationale: An extension inside the server's process can read its memory and crash or stall it, so one bad integration takes the portal down. Backstage's threat model says there is no boundary between plugins on one host.

forged-identity.fix: Trust identity headers only in dev mode, in crates/toolbox-authz/src/authn.rs.
forged-identity.rationale: If the server believes an identity header, any client that reaches it can act as anyone, an operator included. Toolbox's image did this until the comparison found it.

loopback-by-default.fix: Bind 127.0.0.1 unless `--listen` says otherwise, in crates/toolbox-cli/src/main.rs.
loopback-by-default.rationale: A server bound to every interface is reachable from the whole network before anyone has configured its auth. Both products' shipped images listen on every interface, so both fail.

owner-only-fields.fix: Keep facets and their filter guard in crates/toolbox-api/src/access.rs, pinned by crates/toolbox-api/tests/authz.rs.
owner-only-fields.rationale: Without field-level access, a sensitive field is either shown to every signed-in user or kept out of the catalog; a filter that can test a hidden value leaks it anyway.

vs-backstage-security.title: Security defaults

vs-backstage-supply-chain.description: What an adopter inherits: third-party packages, their known vulnerabilities, and whether the release can be verified. OpenSSF and SLSA build provenance.
vs-backstage-supply-chain.rationale: An adopter inherits every package a portal ships, as attack surface and as upgrade work, and runs it next to the catalog and its credentials. Provenance is how they prove that what they deploy was built from the published source.

high-vulnerabilities.fix: Run `osv-scanner scan source --lockfile Cargo.lock` and update or replace the listed packages first.
high-vulnerabilities.rationale: High and critical advisories are the ones a security review blocks a deploy on, and the ones that need a patched release fast; one in the shipped lockfile can keep a portal out of production.

known-vulnerabilities.fix: Run `osv-scanner scan source --lockfile Cargo.lock` and update or replace the listed packages.
known-vulnerabilities.rationale: Each known advisory is a finding the adopter's scanner raises and someone must triage, even when, like Toolbox's unmaintained chrono crates, it is not exploitable.

packages.fix: List the heaviest dependencies with `cargo tree -e normal`, and drop or feature-gate them in Cargo.toml.
packages.rationale: Every third-party package is code an adopter runs, scans and updates without having chosen it, so more packages mean more advisories and more upgrade churn. Backstage's Node runtime is not counted.

provenance.fix: Attest every artifact in .github/workflows/release.yml, and check with `gh attestation verify`.
provenance.rationale: Without verifiable provenance, an adopter cannot tell a release built from the published source from one swapped in the registry or the build system.

vs-backstage-supply-chain.title: Supply chain

vs-backstage.description: Toolbox 581be50 against Backstage 1.57.0: timed factors are medians of 5 scripted runs on a 10,000-component catalog, and on 2026-11-23 an independent agent adjudicator recomputed every number and upheld the verdict. Toolbox 581be50 is a commit after v0.1.1, compiled as a release build, and its install facts come from the published v0.1.1 download; each product was installed as its project documents on one 4 vCPU Intel Xeon VM with Linux 6.12 and one Postgres 16, and the load generator shares the same 4 vCPU. Capability and fact factors are probes and facts with evidence, and the capability scenarios come from the Backstage parity audit, so they favour what Backstage ships. Toolbox's maintainers chose the factors from ISO/IEC 25010's quality characteristics, each with a rule that could show Toolbox worse, and set every rule's bar before the run. Both products are scored on the same rules, factor by factor. The adjudicator was a fresh coding agent outside the benchmark: it designed none of it and decides no rule, so every rule stays measured; it recomputed the numbers from the raw results and checked the scoring.
